look_here_first: Like Texas snakeweed, an open and wispy yellow-flowering annual. Examine the back of a real flower head: pale/resinous phyllaries without green midnerve borders; then the DISC floret has long white basally united pappus scales, unlike G. texana's nearly absent/very short scales. Do not identify this species from habit/color alone; compare A. dracunculoides arrangement too.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — Karst Canyon Preserve vegetation survey records Amphiachyris amoena. Travis — specimen-backed Edwards Plateau record west of Oak Hill. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a dedicated county treatment.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Asteraceae composite heads: ray florets + disc florets inside a phyllary involucre, producing cypselae.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Compared with Amphiachyris dracunculoides, A. amoena is a Texas limestone specialist with very narrow sparse leaves and small resinous heads.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Most important snakeweed double: both A. amoena and G. texana are open-panicle yellow-flowered annuals. A. amoena: whitish phyllary backs without green-lined midnerve and long spatulate-tipped DISC pappus scales, whereas G. texana has variable green-lined phyllary nerves and very short/absent pappus. Distinguish from A. dracunculoides with open versus crowded arrays and fruit rib count/receptacle hairs, not yellow rays.
